ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: From left to right, in the figure the signal m(t) first enters a multiplier, whose lower input is s(t). Then the signal enters an intermediate node/summing node, where n(t) is added from below. Further to the right it enters a second multiplier, whose lower input is also s(t). Finally the signal passes through a Lowpass filter, the filter is labeled with cutoff frequency 1 Hz, and the output is y(t). Reasoning: Use the Fourier transform representation with frequency f. m(t)=2 sin(2πt)/t is a baseband rectangular spectrum, supported on |f|≤1 Hz. n(t)=sin(199πt)/t=sin(2π·99.5t)/t is a rectangular spectrum, supported on |f|≤99.5 Hz. s(t)=cos(200πt)=cos(2π·100t), therefore the first multiplication by s(t) shifts M(f) to two frequency bands centered at ±100 Hz. The intermediate node then adds N(f). After the second multiplication by the same s(t), the m path is equivalent to m(t)cos^2(2π100t), whose low-frequency component is m(t)/2, so the low-pass filtering retains m(t)/2=sin(2πt)/t. The time-domain signal corresponding to these two frequency bands is [sin(0.5πt)/t]cos(1.5πt). Therefore the output is the sum of two parts.

Then the signal enters an intermediate node/summing node, where n(t) is added from below. Further to the right it enters a second multiplier, whose lower input is also s(t). Finally the signal passes through a Lowpass filter, the filter is labeled with cutoff frequency 1 Hz, and the output is y(t). Reasoning: Use the Fourier transform representation with frequency f. m(t)=2 sin(2πt)/t is a baseband rectangular spectrum, supported on |f|≤1 Hz. n(t)=sin(199πt)/t=sin(2π·99.5t)/t is a rectangular spectrum, supported on |f|≤99.5 Hz. s(t)=cos(200πt)=cos(2π·100t), therefore the first multiplication by s(t) shifts M(f) to two frequency bands centered at ±100 Hz. The intermediate node then adds N(f). After the second multiplication by the same s(t), the m path is equivalent to m(t)cos^2(2π100t), whose low-frequency component is m(t)/2, so the low-pass filtering retains m(t)/2=sin(2πt)/t. The n path becomes n(t)cos(2π100t), and its spectrum is N(f) shifted toward ±100 Hz and each multiplied by 1/2; within the low-pass range |f|≤1, only the two segments [0.5,1] and [-1,-0.5] remain. The time-domain signal corresponding to these two frequency bands is [sin(0.5πt)/t]cos(1.5πt). Therefore the output is the sum of two parts.
